title: DeepSWE: A Contamination-Resistant Coding Benchmark — James Shi, Datacurve
talk_summary: Datacurve built DeepSWE, a 113-task coding benchmark authored from scratch across many repositories to resist contamination and reward hacking. The talk details verifier design, prompt style, model behavior, and v1.1 safeguards like separate verifier runtime and trimmed git refs.

takeaways.what_they_do: They author original tasks from scratch instead of mining public PRs, spread tasks across many repos, and use the suite to compare models without leaked solutions or git-history cheating.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we made a decision to want to have every task authored uh from scratch uh rather than being mined
takeaways.numbers: 113 tasks; ~91-100 repos; median 1 task/repo; TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Rust, Go

takeaways.what_they_do: They verify observable behavior and avoid tests tied to specific function names, private helpers, or the merged PR implementation, reducing false negatives.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we want to uh emphasize on the observable behavior as much as possible
takeaways.numbers: They report reduced false negatives and false positives vs SWE-bench Pro using human experts and LLM-as-judge, but cite no exact rates.

takeaways.technique: Separate verifier runtime and strip git refs
takeaways.what_they_do: They run the verifier in a runtime fully separate from the agent runtime, standardize test reports, and remove git refs/commits except the base commit to block reward hacking.
takeaways.evidence_quote: verifier runtime is fully separate now from the agent runtime

takeaways.what_they_do: They use the same agent harness across models to measure base model performance plus token efficiency, cost, token usage, and peak context.
takeaways.numbers: Leaderboard reports token efficiency, cost, token usage, and peak context.

takeaways.technique: Split multi-part requirements; keep prompts high-level
takeaways.what_they_do: They keep task prompts terse and high-level rather than prescriptive to-do lists, but observed Claude dropping one part of multi-part prompts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it becomes quite forgetful when it comes to multi-art prompts
takeaways.numbers: Claude dropped the async part in roughly 2 out of 3 rollouts.

takeaways.what_they_do: They avoid telling agents that tests are handled; stronger models then write/run tests to verify their own work, while a single prompt line suppresses that behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: With that single line in the prompt it will uh prevent the models
takeaways.numbers: Stronger models self-test the majority of the time; weaker models do so far less frequently.
